documents.title: Student Expectations (Using AI Responsibly)
documents.stance_why: The page says "There is no single university-wide policy that determines when AI may be used for coursework. Expectations vary by instructor, assignment, department, and college." It sets no default itself and hands the decision down, so it delegates, even though it warns that unauthorized use may be misconduct.
documents.summary: Student-facing page stating that Iowa has no single university-wide AI policy and that expectations vary by instructor, assignment, department and college. It lists student responsibilities and ties unauthorized AI use to the Academic Misconduct Policy.

units.why: The opening sentence says "There is no single university-wide policy", so the decision is left to others; this is the delegation rule, P04 rather than P85 because the sentence names no unit-level body.
units.anchor: There is no single university-wide policy that determines when AI may be used for coursework.
units.resolution_why: A coded the second sentence ('Expectations vary...') as P04 with actor student; B coded the opening sentence 'There is no single university-wide policy that determines when AI may be used for coursework' as P04 with actor all. Both sentences open the page, and the opening one states the delegation rule, so the final unit anchors on it. The page is student-facing, but the statement describes the whole university and binds no particular group, so actor is all. Type P04 is agreed.

units.why: "Expectations vary by instructor, assignment, department, and college" lets colleges and departments set their own expectations, which is P85 (the instructor and assignment level is already coded in the previous unit).
units.anchor: Expectations vary by instructor, assignment, department, and college.
units.resolution_why: Both coders gave P85 (colleges and departments set their own expectations) to 'Expectations vary by instructor, assignment, department, and college'. They differ on actor (A student, B all); the sentence describes where rules come from rather than telling students to do something, so actor is all. A's normalized policy added 'from the university-wide statement', which the source does not say, so the anchor alone is kept (policy null).

units.why: "review your course syllabus, assignment instructions, and any guidance" tells students to find and follow the rules before using AI, which is P78 (finding out the rules), not P10 (asking when unsure), which is the next sentence.
units.anchor: Before using AI for any assignment, review your course syllabus, assignment instructions
units.policy: Students review their course syllabus, assignment instructions, and any guidance provided by the instructor before using AI for any assignment.
units.resolution_why: A coded phase during-work, B course-start. The source says 'Before using AI for any assignment, review your course syllabus...'; the duty is the student's, triggered when starting work on an assignment, whereas course-start is for communicating expectations (an instructor-side act). Final phase is during-work. Type P78 is agreed; B's normalized policy is faithful to the sentence and kept.

units.why: "If you're unsure whether AI is permitted, ask before submitting your work" is the ask-first rule, P10.
units.anchor: If you're unsure whether AI is permitted, ask before submitting your work.

units.why: "Unauthorized use of AI may be considered academic misconduct" classifies improper AI use as misconduct, P36; "serious academic consequences" is vague so it is not P37.
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of AI may be considered academic misconduct and could result in serious academic
units.resolution_why: Agreed on the codes. A also coded 'could result in serious academic consequences' as a second unit (P36, neutral); that clause is part of the same sentence, names no concrete penalty and says nothing beyond the misconduct classification, so it is folded into this unit with B's longer anchor and A's second unit is dropped.

units.why: "Understanding your instructor's expectations for AI use" makes students responsible for learning the rules; P78.
units.anchor: Understanding your instructor's expectations for AI use.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. Source: the 'Your Responsibilities' list says students are responsible for 'Understanding your instructor's expectations for AI use.' It is a distinct duty (know the instructor's rules), so kept under P78.

units.why: "Following course and assignment-specific policies" makes students responsible for obeying the rules that apply; P78.
units.anchor: Following course and assignment-specific policies.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. Source: 'Following course and assignment-specific policies.' is its own bullet in the student responsibilities list, a duty to obey the applicable rules; kept under P78.

units.why: Under "Your Responsibilities", "Completing your own academic work unless AI use has been authorized" makes students own what they submit, with AI as the authorized exception: P29 (ownership) rather than P19 because it does not list banned tasks.
units.anchor: Completing your own academic work unless AI use has been authorized.
units.fit_note: Also sets a default that AI is out unless authorized (the fallback-rule idea of P06).
units.resolution_why: A coded P06 (fallback when a syllabus is silent), B coded P29 (students own what they submit). The source bullet is 'Completing your own academic work unless AI use has been authorized'; it is a responsibility about the work being the student's own, and it says nothing about what happens when a syllabus is silent. P29 is where a reader would look for it; the 'unless authorized' default is recorded in fit_note.

units.why: "Citing or acknowledging AI use when required" is a conditional disclosure duty, P24.
units.anchor: Citing or acknowledging AI use when required.
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance 'require', B 'permit'. The codebook uses 'permit' for AI allowed with conditions such as disclosure and 'require' only when AI use itself is required; this passage conditions permitted AI use on disclosure, so the final unit_stance is permit.

units.why: "Reviewing AI-generated content for accuracy" tells students to verify output, P31.
units.anchor: Reviewing AI-generated content for accuracy.

units.why: "Protecting sensitive, personal, and university information" is a data-protection duty, P50.
units.anchor: Protecting sensitive, personal, and university information.

units.why: "regularly check on university, collegiate, and instructor guidance to keep up with changes" asks users to stay current, P102.
units.anchor: You should regularly check on university, collegiate, and instructor guidance to keep up with changes.

units.why: The Academic Integrity section says the Academic Misconduct Policy "prohibits the unauthorized use of artificial intelligence tools during academic exercises", an existing integrity rule applied to AI: P36.
units.anchor: Academic Misconduct Policy prohibits the unauthorized use of artificial intelligence tools during academic exercises.
units.resolution_why: A coded actor student and unit_stance restrict; B coded actor all and unit_stance prohibit. The source: the Academic Misconduct Policy 'prohibits the unauthorized use of artificial intelligence tools during academic exercises'. Academic exercises are done by students, so the rule binds students (actor student). It bans only unauthorized use, i.e. AI is out unless authorized, which is the codebook's restrict, not prohibit. B's longer anchor is kept.

units.why: "Using AI in ways that are not permitted by your instructor or course policies may constitute academic misconduct" ties misconduct to instructor permission, P36.
units.anchor: Using AI in ways that are not permitted by your instructor
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this; B's last unit covered the Academic Misconduct Policy sentence only. Source: 'Using AI in ways that are not permitted by your instructor or course policies may constitute academic misconduct' is a separate sentence in the Academic Integrity section and ties misconduct to instructor permission; kept as P36.

units.why: "Consider ... opportunities for your students to use and learn about AI" suggests teaching AI use as a course aim, close to P44 though not framed as a career skill.
units.anchor: if there are opportunities for your students to use and learn about AI
units.fit_note: Phrased as 'Consider ... opportunities ... to use and learn about AI' tied to the course's learning objectives; no professional-skill framing.
units.resolution_why: A coded P83 (align with learning objectives) and cited the 'keep your course goals and values in mind' sentence; B split that sentence out as its own P83 unit and coded this one, 'Consider ... if there are opportunities for your students to use and learn about AI that align with the learning objectives of the course', as P44. The goals/values sentence is kept as the P83 unit. This sentence adds something different, namely that students might use and learn about AI in the course, so P44 (teaching AI use) with encourage, and the fit_note records that the source ties it to learning objectives rather than to a professional skill.

The addressee is the instructor, who must make sure students know this, so actor is instructor, and as instructor-addressed guidance it takes no position on AI use itself (neutral). Type P24 and modality must are agreed; the fit note stands.

units.resolution_why: A coded may/P09, B coded informs/P63. The source says the webpage 'has sample policy language ... that you can incorporate into your syllabus'. The sentence tells instructors they can use ready language, which is 'may'. P63 is about supporting faculty in learning AI, while this resource exists to help write the syllabus AI statement (P09); fit_note records that nothing is required.

documents.summary: Teaching-office article urging instructors to state AI expectations in the syllabus, repeat them in each assignment, and explain how students should cite or disclose AI use. It offers task-by-task examples, the AI Assessment Scale and a sample disclosure statement.

units.why: "Clearly stating your expectations around AI use in your syllabus fosters academic integrity, reduces confusion" recommends a syllabus statement and gives the reason; P09.
units.anchor: Clearly stating your expectations around AI use in your syllabus
units.frag_end: sets your learning community up for success.

units.why: "AI expectations should also be discussed in class" asks instructors to talk the rules through with students, P66; the extra ask to add them to assignments is coded separately.
units.anchor: AI expectations should also be discussed in class

units.why: 'AI expectations should also be discussed in class and added into individual assignment descriptions' asks instructors to state the AI expectation in each assignment description, the same statement duty as P09 applied per assignment.
units.anchor: added into individual assignment descriptions
units.policy: AI expectations are added to individual assignment descriptions so students understand what is appropriate task by task.
units.fit_note: Assignment-level rather than syllabus-level statement.
units.resolution_why: Only A coded this half of the sentence (B coded 'discussed in class' as P66 and left out 'added into individual assignment descriptions'). Source: 'AI expectations should also be discussed in class and added into individual assignment descriptions to help students understand what's appropriate task by task.' Adding the rule to assignment descriptions is a second, separate recommendation, so kept. A coded it P04; since it asks instructors to write the expectation down rather than leaving the rule to them, P09 (as B did for the similar 'Add brief explanations' sentence) is the better fit.

units.why: "Be clear with students about when, how, and why AI tools may or may not be used" asks for the rule and its reasons in the syllabus; P09.
units.anchor: when, how, and why AI tools may or may not be used
units.frag_end: may or may not be used.
units.policy: Instructors are clear with students about when, how, and why AI tools may or may not be used.
units.fit_note: Also asks for the reasons behind the rule.
units.resolution_why: A coded P09, B coded P66 (explain and discuss the rules). The source: 'Be clear with students about when, how, and why AI tools may or may not be used', in a list on stating expectations in the syllabus. It asks that the expectation and its reasons be stated, which is the syllabus statement; the discussion in class is the previous unit (P66). Final P09, fit_note keeps the 'why' element.

units.why: "Connect your course policies to your course's learning outcomes" bases AI decisions on learning outcomes, P83.
units.anchor: Connect your course policies to your course's learning outcomes

units.why: "include specific language about academic misconduct" and that unauthorized use "may be considered a violation" of the Code of Student Life tells limiting instructors to name misconduct consequences; P36.
units.anchor: include specific language about academic misconduct
units.fit_note: Advises instructors to put the misconduct language in the syllabus.
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance restrict, B neutral. The source: 'If you choose to set limits around student AI use, include specific language about academic misconduct and note ... the Code of Student Life'. It advises instructors how to word a limit if they set one and sets no limit itself, so neutral. A's second unit on the clause 'If you choose to set limits around student AI use' (P04) is dropped: it is the condition of this same sentence, not a separate rule.

units.why: "Revisit your expectations throughout the semester" asks instructors to keep the expectations under review, P54.
units.anchor: Revisit your expectations throughout the semester.
units.fit_note: Revisiting expectations with students during the term, not revising the policy itself.

units.why: 'Students are likely encountering very different AI expectations across multiple instructors and disciplines' describes rules differing by instructor and discipline. P04 (each instructor sets the rule) is the nearest type, though the sentence states a fact rather than delegating.
units.anchor: Students are likely encountering very different AI expectations across multiple instructors and disciplines.
units.fit_note: Describes the variation in expectations as a fact; it does not itself hand the decision to instructors.
units.resolution_why: A coded actor instructor and P11 (each course's policy governs only that course); B coded actor all and P04. The source sentence says students meet different expectations across instructors; it never says a permission does not carry over from one course to another, which is what P11 means. P04 is nearer (rules set by instructor), with a fit_note. The sentence describes students' situation and is not addressed to instructors, so actor is all.

units.resolution_why: A coded P04, B coded P09. The source tells instructors to add explanations to assignment descriptions; it asks them to state the rule, not to leave the rule to them, which is the P09 duty (kept with a fit_note for assignment-level).

units.why: "consider providing step-by-step guidance that explicitly addresses AI use at each stage and why" suggests separate AI rules per stage of a task; P35.

AI should not be used for this step', so the wording is 'should not' (should-not). It bans AI for this one step, not 'unless permitted', so unit_stance prohibit. Type P19 agreed.

units.why: Drafting example: "AI can assist in outlining or organizing ideas" permits outlining support; P91.

Source: 'AI can assist in outlining or organizing ideas, but core arguments and analysis must be the student's own.' The 'may use AI to outline' rule and the 'core arguments must be the student's own' rule are two distinct rules, so they are two units.

units.why: Reviewing example: "Peer feedback must reflect the student's own thinking. AI should not be used during peer review" keeps the student as thinker: P32.
units.anchor: AI should not be used during peer review.

units.resolution_why: A coded P19 should-not/restrict, B P32 must-not/prohibit. The source: 'Peer feedback must reflect the student's own thinking. AI should not be used during peer review.' The wording of the AI rule is 'should not' (should-not); it bans AI for this stage (prohibit). The reason given is that the student remains the thinker, so P32 (students stay the primary problem-solver) fits better than P19, which is about not submitting AI-produced work.

units.why: Revising example: "AI may be used for grammatical and spelling errors" permits editing support; P91.
units.anchor: AI may be used for grammatical and spelling errors.

units.why: "Submit a before and after editing draft for this stage" requires drafts as evidence of AI editing, P26.
units.anchor: Submit a before and after editing draft for this stage of the assignment.
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance 'require', B 'permit'. The codebook uses 'permit' for AI allowed with conditions such as disclosure and 'require' only when AI use itself is required; this passage conditions permitted AI use on disclosure, so the final unit_stance is permit.

units.why: The page recommends "The AI Assessment Scale (Perkins & Furze)" as a way to label assignments, a set of named levels: P05.

units.resolution_why: A coded modality may, B should. The source: 'The AI Assessment Scale ... is a helpful tool for communicating expectations ... Consider using it to spark classroom conversations or in labelling your assignments accordingly.' 'Consider using' is a recommendation, so should. B's normalized policy is faithful and kept.

units.why: "instructors should help students understand two options in documenting AI use: AI citations and AI disclosures" asks instructors to teach how to acknowledge AI; P24.
units.anchor: instructors should help students understand two options in documenting AI use
units.fit_note: Addressed to instructors: explain citation and disclosure options.
units.resolution_why: A coded unit_stance neutral, B permit. Instructor-addressed teaching advice ('instructors should help students understand two options in documenting AI use') takes no position on AI use itself, so neutral.

units.resolution_why: Only A coded this. Source: 'Similar to citing a conversation with a colleague, the source can't be retrieved, but the influence should be acknowledged.' It treats AI like a human source under citation norms (P45); kept.

documents.title: Teaching With AI
documents.stance_why: The page tells instructors to "set clear expectations for student use" and offers sample syllabus language for "When AI is prohibited," "allowed with attribution" and "encouraged." It chooses none of these for the university, so it delegates, with risk tiers for instructor uses.

documents.summary: Instructor-facing page on teaching with AI: recommended tools and use cases, risk-rated Q&A on instructor uses, syllabus sample language for prohibit, attribute and encourage options, and advice on detectors, assessment design, AI browsers and smart glasses. It sets no student default and tells instructors to set clear expectations.

notes: Merged from coders A and B (A: 171 units, B: 108). Computing layer none-found and course layer deferred per the collect file. Topic codes are mapped to the starter codebook in tools/AGENT_BRIEF.md (coder A had used free labels). Sample syllabus language in the Teaching With AI page is coded as templates offered to instructors, not Iowa rules (fit notes say where they come from). The CLAS memo's sanctions and reporting rules (P37, P80, P81, P64) are general academic-misconduct rules, coded because the memo is the college's AI-misconduct guidance. Units dropped after checking the source: student-expectations 'could result in serious academic consequences' (same sentence as the P36 unit; A's fit note: warns of unspecified serious consequences, P37 needs concrete penalties) and 'AI is a rapidly developing technology' (A P54, fit note: only notes that guidance will change, promises no review; it is the reason clause of the P102 sentence); OTLT article: 'If you choose to set limits around student AI use' (condition of the misconduct-language sentence), 'avoid unintentional academic misconduct' (rationale clause, covered by the closing P99 unit), the list of external disclosure style guides (links only), and the scene-setting sentence 'Generative AI tools are reshaping how students study, write, and learn' (A UNCOVERED, note: scene-setting statement with no rule attached; not a policy); Teaching With AI page: 'hiring a person or a company to write essays' (sample-template wording not about AI), the detector reading list, the Gradescope sentence (grading tool, not about AI) and the pointer to the chatbot guidance page (navigation). Fit notes of the last two dropped units: detector reading list (cites research on detector accuracy, not on how AI affects learning) and Gradescope (mentions paper-based tests as an option; no shift in weight is stated).
